title: May and might: future possibilities and alternatives
summary: Use may and might for future events that remain possible rather than settled, including possible obligations, abilities and activities in progress. Use might in unreal conditions and might as well when one choice makes sense because there is no better alternative.
learningObjectives: Talk about uncertain future events and plans with may/might (not) + base verb, contrasting them with a settled intention.
Use may/might have to and may/might be able to for possible future necessity and ability.
Use may/might be + -ing for uncertain future activities, distinguishing it from a definite future continuous statement.
Use might in an unreal conditional situation and explain the practical meaning of might/may as well.

explanation.heading: Uncertain future decisions and happenings
explanation.body: May or might + base verb expresses a future option or event without announcing a definite plan. Use the negative may not or might not when something may fail to happen. These forms can refer to decisions that have not yet been made or changes outside the speaker’s control. By contrast, be going to generally presents an intention already formed. Both may and might are common for future possibilities.
explanation.example: I might take the evening train, but I have not booked anything yet.

explanation.heading: Possible need and possible ability
explanation.body: Use may/might have to + base verb when it is possible that an obligation will arise. Use may/might be able to + base verb when someone could have the opportunity or ability to do something. The word have in might have to is not the perfect auxiliary: it means necessity here. The time context makes clear that the possibility concerns the future.
explanation.example: If the delivery is late, we might have to move the appointment.

explanation.heading: Activities that may be happening later
explanation.body: Use may/might be + -ing when an activity could be in progress at a particular future time or may form part of an uncertain plan. Will be + -ing is more definite: the speaker presents the future activity as expected, while might be + -ing does not commit to it. Mention the future time to make the intended meaning clear.
explanation.example: At eight tomorrow evening, the volunteers may be setting up the exhibition.

explanation.heading: Might in an imagined condition
explanation.body: Might can appear in the result of an unreal or hypothetical condition: If I lived closer, I might cycle to work. The if-clause uses a past-form verb to describe an imagined present situation, not a known past event. In this pattern might is the natural choice; do not replace it with may in the same hypothetical meaning. Do not confuse this with an ordinary future possibility.
explanation.example: If the flat had a balcony, I might grow vegetables there.

explanation.heading: Might as well: a reasonable choice without a better option
explanation.body: Might as well + base verb suggests doing something because no better practical alternative exists or there is no good reason to delay it. May as well has the same core meaning. It is not simply a prediction that the action may happen; the speaker is effectively proposing a sensible course of action. The reason should be clear from the situation.
explanation.example: The next ferry is two hours away, so we might as well have lunch nearby.

comparisons.title: A firm future arrangement versus an open option

left.label: Settled intention
left.example: We are going to rent a small car for the trip.
left.note: The speaker presents a decision that has already been made.

right.label: Uncertain option
right.example: We might rent a small car for the trip.

comparisons.title: A possible activity later versus a practical suggestion now

left.label: Might be + -ing
left.example: At six tomorrow, we might be travelling through the hills.

right.label: Might as well + base verb
right.example: The last train has gone; we might as well stay overnight.
right.note: The speaker recommends a sensible alternative given the circumstances.

examples.sentence: The weather may improve before the concert starts.
examples.note: May improve describes an uncertain future development.

examples.sentence: Dina might not attend the workshop if her shift runs late.
examples.note: Might not attend allows for an uncertain negative future outcome.

examples.sentence: We may have to pay a small fee when we collect the tickets.
examples.note: May have to shows that an obligation could arise later.

examples.sentence: I might be able to join the call after my appointment.
examples.note: Might be able to expresses uncertain future availability.

examples.sentence: If the garden were bigger, we might put a bench under the trees.
examples.note: Might introduces a possible result in an imagined situation.

commonMistakes.incorrect: I might to visit the museum this weekend.
commonMistakes.correct: I might visit the museum this weekend.
commonMistakes.why: A modal takes the base form visit without to.

commonMistakes.incorrect: If I owned a motorbike, I may ride to the coast every weekend.
commonMistakes.correct: If I owned a motorbike, I might ride to the coast every weekend.
commonMistakes.why: In this unreal conditional result, use might rather than may.

commonMistakes.incorrect: We might be able finish the repairs tomorrow.
commonMistakes.correct: We might be able to finish the repairs tomorrow.
commonMistakes.why: Be able takes to + base verb: be able to finish.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The bus leaves in an hour, so we might as well waiting here.
commonMistakes.correct: The bus leaves in an hour, so we might as well wait here.
commonMistakes.why: Might as well is followed by the base verb wait, not an -ing form.

studyTips: Label future statements as decided, uncertain, or hypothetical; then choose be going to, may/might, or if + past form ... might accordingly.
Write one pair using might have to and might be able to, and explain which expresses a possible obligation and which a possible opportunity.
Invent a short situation with no attractive alternative, then complete “We might as well ...” with a base verb and a sensible action.

exercises.prompt: Nadia has not decided about Saturday and has made no reservations. Which sentence keeps the plan uncertain?
choices: Nadia is definitely visiting the island.
Nadia might visit the island.
Nadia visited the island last Saturday.
exercises.feedback: Might visit describes an open future option rather than a settled plan or a past event.

exercises.prompt: The queue may be long tomorrow. We ___ outside until the doors open.
choices: might have to wait
might have waited
might to wait
exercises.feedback: Might have to wait means a waiting obligation could arise in the future.

exercises.prompt: A technician has offered to examine the computer tomorrow. She ___ it before lunch, but she cannot promise.
choices: might able repair
might have to repair
might be able to repair
exercises.feedback: Might be able to repair expresses an uncertain future possibility of success.

exercises.prompt: Imagine you worked only four days a week, but in fact you work five. “If I worked four days a week, I ___ more time for music.”
choices: may having
might have
might have had
exercises.feedback: Might have fits the imagined present condition; may is not the usual modal in this unreal result.

exercises.prompt: The plans are not fixed. “We ___ (meet) our cousins next weekend.” Use might for an uncertain future event.
acceptedAnswers: might meet
exercises.feedback: Might meet keeps the future visit undecided.

exercises.prompt: A strike is possible, and travel plans may change. “We ___ (not / travel) on Friday.” Use may.
acceptedAnswers: may not travel
exercises.feedback: May not travel expresses an uncertain negative future outcome.

exercises.prompt: The repairs are nearly finished, but success is not certain. “We ___ (finish) by Thursday.” Use might be able to.
acceptedAnswers: might be able to finish
exercises.feedback: Might be able to finish describes possible future ability to complete the work.

exercises.prompt: The last café has closed and it is raining heavily; staying indoors is the sensible choice. “We ___ (stay) here until the rain stops.” Use might as well.
acceptedAnswers: might as well stay
exercises.feedback: Might as well stay recommends a practical option when going elsewhere is unappealing.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: They might visiting the coast next month, but they have not decided.
acceptedAnswers: They might visit the coast next month, but they have not decided.
exercises.feedback: For an ordinary future possibility, might is followed by the base verb visit.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: If I lived nearer the station, I may walk there every morning.
acceptedAnswers: If I lived nearer the station, I might walk there every morning.
exercises.feedback: The unreal condition uses might for its imagined result rather than may.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: We may have pay for parking when the new rules start.
acceptedAnswers: We may have to pay for parking when the new rules start.
exercises.feedback: Possible future necessity takes may have to + base verb pay.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: The exhibition is free today, so we might as well going inside.
acceptedAnswers: The exhibition is free today, so we might as well go inside.
exercises.feedback: Might as well is followed by the base form go to propose a sensible action.

speakingExercises.prompt: The trip has not been arranged. Say one sentence beginning “We” and using “might visit the coast next month”.
acceptedAnswers: We might visit the coast next month.
speakingExercises.feedback: Might visit expresses a possible future plan, not a decision already made.

speakingExercises.prompt: It is uncertain whether Iris will arrive on time tomorrow. Say one negative future possibility beginning “Iris” and using “may not arrive on time tomorrow”.
acceptedAnswers: Iris may not arrive on time tomorrow.
speakingExercises.feedback: May not arrive presents lateness as a possibility, not a certainty.

speakingExercises.prompt: The event may run late. Say a possible future obligation with exactly “We might have to leave early”.
acceptedAnswers: We might have to leave early.
speakingExercises.feedback: Might have to presents an obligation that could arise.

speakingExercises.prompt: A colleague may be free on Friday. Say one sentence beginning “She” and using “might be able to help on Friday”.
acceptedAnswers: She might be able to help on Friday.
speakingExercises.feedback: Might be able to expresses possible future availability or ability.

speakingExercises.prompt: Describe an uncertain activity at nine tomorrow morning. Begin with “The students” and use “might be taking the exam at nine tomorrow morning”.
acceptedAnswers: The students might be taking the exam at nine tomorrow morning.
speakingExercises.feedback: Might be taking describes an activity that may be in progress at the stated future time.

speakingExercises.prompt: Imagine you had a larger kitchen, but you do not. Make one sentence beginning “If I had a larger kitchen,” followed by “I might cook more often”.
acceptedAnswers: If I had a larger kitchen, I might cook more often.
speakingExercises.feedback: An unreal condition combines if + past form with might for an imagined result.

speakingExercises.prompt: The next bus will not come for ninety minutes, and the café is nearby. Suggest the practical alternative. Begin “We” and use “might as well walk to the café”.
acceptedAnswers: We might as well walk to the café.
speakingExercises.feedback: Might as well recommends an available option because waiting offers little benefit.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say exactly two sentences. First, report this decided plan: “I am going to visit the gallery on Saturday.” Second, report this open option: “I might visit the museum on Sunday.”
acceptedAnswers: I am going to visit the gallery on Saturday. I might visit the museum on Sunday.
I’m going to visit the gallery on Saturday. I might visit the museum on Sunday.
speakingExercises.feedback: Going to expresses a settled intention; might visit leaves the other visit undecided.

listeningExercises.prompt: What is the speaker’s plan for the weekend?
choices: The speaker has two possibilities but no firm plan.
The speaker has booked a lakeside hotel.
The speaker has cancelled a holiday already booked.
listeningExercises.feedback: Might go and might stay show alternatives that have not been decided.
listeningExercises.audioText: I have not booked a trip yet. I might go to the lake this weekend, or I might stay home.

listeningExercises.prompt: What possible problem does the speaker anticipate?
choices: The car has already broken down.
They may need to change their route.
The journey is definitely cancelled.
listeningExercises.feedback: Might have to indicates that choosing another route could become necessary.
listeningExercises.audioText: The roadworks may continue on Monday, so we might have to take another route.

listeningExercises.prompt: Type the three-word modal verb phrase immediately after “I”.
acceptedAnswers: may not travel
listeningExercises.feedback: May not travel expresses a possible negative future outcome.
listeningExercises.audioText: I may not travel on Sunday if the weather remains dangerous.

listeningExercises.prompt: What is uncertain about four o’clock tomorrow?
choices: Whether the event happened yesterday.
Whether the speaker has answered questions already.
Whether she will be answering questions then.
listeningExercises.feedback: Might be answering refers to an activity that could be underway at a future time.
listeningExercises.audioText: The guest speaker has not confirmed, but she might be answering questions at four tomorrow.

choices: The speaker is describing an imagined situation.
The speaker cycles to that nearby office every day.
The office has already moved closer.
listeningExercises.feedback: If the office were nearer presents an unreal condition; might cycle gives its imagined result.
listeningExercises.audioText: If the office were nearer my home, I might cycle there instead of driving.

listeningExercises.prompt: Why does the speaker suggest leaving?
choices: They have confirmed a delayed train.
There is little reason to remain at the museum.
They still have several hours to look around.
listeningExercises.feedback: Might as well proposes the practical choice because the museum is about to close.
listeningExercises.audioText: The museum is closing in five minutes, so we might as well head to the station now.

listeningExercises.prompt: Type the four-word modal expression immediately after “We”.
acceptedAnswers: might have to use
listeningExercises.feedback: Might have to use indicates an obligation that may arise tomorrow.
listeningExercises.audioText: The lift is out of service today. We might have to use the stairs tomorrow too.

listeningExercises.prompt: Type the four-word modal expression immediately after “we”.
acceptedAnswers: might as well start
listeningExercises.feedback: Might as well start suggests beginning because waiting offers no obvious advantage.
listeningExercises.audioText: The audience is small, but we might as well start the presentation now.
